title: Exploding stars appear to keep an entire galaxy’s gas stirred up
freshness: Published September 17, 2026 — within the preferred 15-day freshness window.
excerpt: Astronomers mapped 118 enormous bubbles in the Andromeda galaxy, blown into its gas by groups of exploding stars. The energy carried by those bubbles closely matches the energy needed to keep Andromeda’s gas in constant turbulent motion.
whyItMatters: Astronomers have long suspected that exploding stars help churn the gas inside galaxies, but proving they can power that motion across a whole galaxy has been difficult. Andromeda now provides direct evidence that generations of dying stars can continually reshape the gas from which future stars are born, linking stellar death to the ongoing evolution of a galaxy.

## A hundred and eighteen bubbles, and a budget that matches

Astronomers mapped 118 enormous bubbles in the Andromeda galaxy, blown into the gas by groups of exploding stars. The energy those bubbles carry lines up with the energy required to keep Andromeda’s gas turbulent. The paper is in Nature Astronomy, published 17 September 2026: “Supernova origin of galactic turbulence revealed by superbubbles.” Tsinghua University’s note, “Superbubbles drive turbulence in the Andromeda galaxy,” is the other source.

Turbulence here is not a metaphor. Gas in a galaxy moves in disordered flows at many scales. That motion holds clouds up, sets how fast they collapse into stars, and mixes metals from dead stars into the next generation. Something has to keep driving it. Ordered rotation does not, by itself, maintain a galaxy-wide fizz. The drivers usually on the list are gravity, magnetic fields, inflowing gas, and stellar feedback — winds and supernovae from massive stars. Proving one of them can carry the whole budget, across a whole galaxy, has been the hard part. A simulation can be told to do it. A galaxy has to be mapped.

## What a superbubble is

One supernova digs a cavity. A group of massive stars, born together, explodes over a few million years and the cavities merge. The result is a superbubble: a shell of swept-up gas around a hotter, thinner interior, tens or hundreds of light-years across, sometimes more. Andromeda is close enough, and inclined in a way that helps, that 118 of these shells can be picked out and their energies added up. The sum matching the turbulent energy is the result. “Closely matches” is the notebook’s wording and should stay at that precision. This note will not invent a percentage.

The match is what lets the authors say the supernovae are sufficient, not merely present. Sufficiency is still a step. Other drivers could contribute, and the bubbles could be the visible part of a mix. The paper’s title is stronger than “contribute.” It says the origin is revealed, and that the origin is supernovae, via the superbubbles. A reader who wants the error bars and the alternative drivers belongs in the Nature Astronomy article. Tsinghua’s note is the group’s own summary of the same map.

## Death as a supply of motion

The loop is why this is more than a gas-dynamics paper. Stars form from the gas. The massive ones die and stir the gas. The stirred gas forms the next stars, with a different efficiency than still gas would have had. Andromeda is one galaxy, a spiral we can resolve, not a cosmic average. The hydrogen note in this notebook is the average: star formation down, atomic gas still around, efficiency as the suspect. Andromeda is a look at one machine that can change that efficiency, running in a neighbor we can actually dissect.

118 is a counted population. It is not “all the feedback in Andromeda,” and it is not a claim about every spiral. A dwarf galaxy, or a galaxy with a violent black hole, may balance its turbulence differently. The scope is this map, this energy comparison, this galaxy.

If you only keep two sentences: groups of exploding stars have inflated 118 giant bubbles in Andromeda’s gas, and the energy in those bubbles is about what the galaxy’s turbulence requires. The first sentence is the map. The second is the comparison the authors use to name the driver. Both live in the paper. The superbubble, as an object, is the thing to look at next — a cavity made by a crowd of massive stars, not by one explosion, and large enough that the motion it leaves behind is a galactic fact rather than a local scar.
